Alright, let's move on to the second approach to clustering: **hierarchical clustering**. And the idea here is beautifully simple. Here's the algorithm, in three steps.

Step one: start by assigning each item to its own cluster. So if you have N items, you now have N clusters, each containing just one item. Step two: find the closest — that is, the most similar — pair of clusters, and merge them into a single cluster. So now you have one fewer cluster than you did before. And step three: just continue that process, merging the closest pair over and over, until all the items are clustered into a single cluster of size N.

So you go from N clusters, to N minus one, to N minus two, all the way down to one. But notice the question sitting at the bottom of this slide: what does distance mean? I told you to merge the "closest" pair of clusters — but when each cluster might contain many points, what's the distance between two *clusters*? That's the key question, and it's what we look at next.

There are several standard ways to define it, and they're called **linkage metrics**.

The first is **single-linkage**: here, the distance between one cluster and another cluster is defined to be equal to the *shortest* distance from any member of one cluster to any member of the other cluster. So the clusters are as close as their nearest pair of points.

The second is **complete-linkage**: here the distance between one cluster and another is the *greatest* distance from any member of one cluster to any member of the other. Now the clusters are only as close as their farthest-apart pair of points.

And the third is **average-linkage**: as you might guess, we take the *average* distance from any member of one cluster to any member of the other.

Different choices of linkage will give you different clusterings, and let's see that concretely with an example.

Here's a table of distances between six American cities: Boston, New York, Chicago, Denver, San Francisco, and Seattle. Reading a few off: Boston to New York is 206 miles — they're very close. Boston to Chicago is 963, Boston to Denver is 1949, Boston to San Francisco is 3095, and Boston to Seattle is 2979. New York to Chicago is 802, New York to Denver is 1771, New York to San Francisco is 2934, New York to Seattle is 2815. Chicago to Denver is 966, Chicago to San Francisco is 2142, Chicago to Seattle is 2013. Denver to San Francisco is 1235, Denver to Seattle is 1307. And San Francisco to Seattle is 808.

Now let's run the algorithm. We start with six singleton clusters: {BOS}, {NY}, {CHI}, {DEN}, {SF}, {SEA}. What's the closest pair? Boston and New York, at 206. So we merge them: {BOS, NY}, {CHI}, {DEN}, {SF}, {SEA}. Next, the closest distance remaining is 802 — New York to Chicago. So Chicago joins the eastern cluster: {BOS, NY, CHI}, {DEN}, {SF}, {SEA}. Then 808 — San Francisco and Seattle merge: {BOS, NY, CHI}, {DEN}, {SF, SEA}.

And now watch what happens — this is where the linkage metric matters. We have {BOS, NY, CHI}, {DEN}, and {SF, SEA}. With **single linkage**, Denver ends up joining the eastern cluster, giving us {BOS, NY, CHI, DEN} and {SF, SEA}. But with **complete linkage**, we get a different answer: Denver instead joins the western cluster, giving {BOS, NY, CHI} and {DEN, SF, SEA}. Same data, same algorithm — but a different notion of "distance between clusters" changes the outcome. That's why you have to think about which linkage is appropriate for your problem.

So, stepping back and comparing our clustering algorithms: hierarchical clustering has some nice properties. You can select the number of clusters after the fact using a **dendrogram** — you can look at the tree of merges and decide where to cut it. It's **deterministic** — same input, same output, every time. And it's **flexible** with respect to the linkage criteria — you can plug in single, complete, or average linkage. The downside? It's **slow**. The naïve algorithm is order n cubed, though n squared algorithms do exist for some linkage criteria.

By contrast, **k-means** is a much faster, greedy algorithm. It's most useful when you know how many clusters you want — that's the k, right there in the name.

So how does k-means work? Here's the pseudocode. First, randomly choose k examples as the initial centroids. Then we loop: create k clusters by assigning each example to its closest centroid. Then compute k new centroids by averaging the examples in each cluster. And if the centroids don't change, we break out of the loop — we've converged.

Now, a question for you: what is the complexity of one iteration of this loop? Think about it — for each of the n points, we compare it against each of the k centroids, and each comparison costs whatever it takes to compute a distance between a pair of points. So the answer is k times n times d, where n is the number of points and d is the time required to compute the distance between a pair of points. That's why k-means is so much faster than hierarchical clustering — and why, when you have a big dataset and a good guess for k, it's usually the tool to reach for.

## Dendrogram
A dendrogram is a diagram representing a tree graph . This diagrammatic representation is frequently used in different contexts: The name dendrogram derives from the two ancient greek words δένδρον ( déndron ), meaning "tree", and γράμμα ( grámma ), meaning "drawing, mathematical figure".   For a clustering example, suppose that five taxa ( a {\displaystyle a} to e {\displaystyle e} ) have been clustered by UPGMA based on a matrix of genetic distances . The hierarchical clustering dendrogram would show a column of five nodes representing the initial data (here individual taxa), and the remaining nodes represent the clusters to which the data belong, with the arrows representing the distance (dissimilarity). The distance between merged clusters is monotone, increasing with the level of the merger: the height of each node in the plot is proportional to the value of the intergroup dissimilarity between its two daughters (the nodes on the right representing individual observations all plotted at zero height).

## K-means clustering
k -means clustering is a method of vector quantization , originally from signal processing , that aims to partition n observations into k clusters in which each observation belongs to the cluster with the nearest mean (cluster centers or cluster centroid ). This results in a partitioning of the data space into Voronoi cells . k -means clustering minimizes within-cluster variances ( squared Euclidean distances ), but not regular Euclidean distances, which would be the more difficult Weber problem : the mean optimizes squared errors, whereas only the geometric median minimizes Euclidean distances. For instance, better Euclidean solutions can be found using k -medians and k -medoids . The problem is computationally difficult ( NP-hard ); however, efficient heuristic algorithms converge quickly to a local optimum . These are usually similar to the expectation–maximization algorithm for mixtures of Gaussian distributions via an iterative refinement approach employed by both k-means and Gaussian mixture modeling . They both use cluster centers to model the data; however, k -means clustering tends to find clusters of comparable spatial extent, while the Gaussian mixture model allows clusters to have different shapes. The unsupervised k -means algorithm has a loose relationship to the k -nearest neighbor classifier , a popular supervised machine learning technique for classification that is often confused with k -means due to the name. Applying the 1-nearest neighbor classifier to the cluster centers obtained by k -means classifies new data into the existing clusters. This is known as nearest centroid classifier or Rocchio algorithm . Given a set of observations ( x 1 , x 2 , ..., x n ) , where each observation is a d {\displaystyle d} -dimensional real vector, k -means clustering aims to partition the n observations into k ( ≤ n ) sets S = { S 1 , S 2 , ..., S k } so as to minimize the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS) (i.e. variance ). This is equivalent to minimizing the pairwise squared deviations of points in the same cluster: a r g m i n S ⁡ ∑ i = 1 k 1 | S i | ∑ x , y ∈ S i ‖ x − y ‖ 2 {\displaystyle \mathop {\operatorname {arg\,min} } _{\mathbf {S} }\sum _{i=1}^{k}\,{\frac {1}{|S_{i}|}}\,\sum _{\mathbf {x} ,\mathbf {y} \in S_{i}}\left\|\mathbf {x} -\mathbf {y} \right\|^{2}} The equivalence can be deduced from the identity | S i | ∑ x ∈ S i ‖ x − μ i ‖ 2 = 1 2 ∑ x , y ∈ S i ‖ x − y ‖ 2 {\textstyle |S_{i}|\sum _{\mathbf {x} \in S_{i}}\left\|\mathbf {x} -{\boldsymbol {\mu }}_{i}\right\|^{2}={\frac {1}{2}}\sum _{\mathbf {x} ,\mathbf {y} \in S_{i}}\left\|\mathbf {x} -\mathbf {y} \right\|^{2}} . Since the total variance is constant, this is equivalent to maximizing the sum of squared deviations between points in different clusters (between-cluster sum of squares, BCSS).  This deterministic relationship is also related to the law of total variance in probability theory. The term " k -means" was first used by James MacQueen in 1967,  though the idea goes back to Hugo Steinhaus in 1956.  The standard algorithm was first proposed by Stuart Lloyd of Bell Labs in 1957 as a technique for pulse-code modulation , although it was not published as a journal article until 1982.  In 1965, Edward W. Forgy published essentially the same method, which is why it is sometimes referred to as the Lloyd–Forgy algorithm.  Early applications of the k-means algorithm were primarily found in signal processing and data compression, particularly in the context of vector quantization . Lloyd's work at Bell Labs focused on representing analog signals using a limited set of discrete values, where clustering was used to reduce the amount of data required while preserving signal quality.  As computing power increased, k-means clustering became widely used in pattern recognition and statistical classification due to its simplicity and computational efficiency. It was later adopted in early machine learning and data analysis tasks involving large datasets.  Despite its widespread use, limitations such as sensitivity to initial centroid placement and difficulty handling non-spherical clusters were recognized early on, motivating the development of improved clustering methods and initialization techniques. Numerous extensions of k-means have since been developed to address limitations of the original algorithm, including methods such as fuzzy c-means, which allows data points to belong to multiple clusters with varying degrees of membership, and kernel k-means, which uses kernel functions to identify non-linearly separable clusters.  The most common algorithm uses an iterative refinement technique. Due to its ubiquity, it is often called "the k -means algorithm"; it is also referred to as Lloyd's algorithm , particularly in the computer science community. It is sometimes also referred to as "naïve k -means", because there exist much faster alternatives.
